en: We praise Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers, from whose opening and closing of his eyes arise the dissolution and emergence of the world; he is the primary outflow [of consciousness]. // 1 //
In that wherein all this effect resides and from which it has emerged, there is no cessation anywhere because its nature is unobstructed. // 2 //
Even as it extends through the various states such as waking and so forth, which are not distinct from it,
it never departs from its own inherent nature as the perceiver.

The cognitions "I am happy," "I am suffering," and "I am attached" clearly occur in relation to something other [than the states themselves], which persists through the various conditions such as happiness and so forth. (4)
Where there is neither suffering nor happiness, neither the grasped nor the grasper, and even no state of delusion—that exists from the perspective of ultimate reality. // 5 //
For this group of instruments, though itself deluded, acts as if undeluded;
together with the internal wheel, it effects manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
One should diligently and with respect examine that reality through such effort,
because his sovereignty in all matters is this very unconditioned state.
For this [scripture] does not function as an impeller by means of a desire to act;
rather, through contact with its own power, a person becomes equal to it.
When the agitation of one who is incapable due to his own impurity, yet desirous of performing his duties,
dissolves away, then the supreme state shall be attained.
Then his dharma is unconditioned, characterized by the nature of knowing and acting;
for he knows and performs everything that is desired.
For one who, beholding that very nature as the state of the presiding subject, remains as if smiling, from where could such a deceptive path arise? (11)

Non-existence does not become something that can be cultivated, nor is there freedom from delusion regarding it; for the certainty that "it was accomplished" arises only through contact with diligent application.

Therefore, that [state] should always be known as artificial, like the state of deep sleep; however, being merely remembered in this way, it does not attain the status of ultimate reality (tattva). // 13 //
And here there are two states designated as "being the effect" and "being the agent.
Among these, the state of being an effect is perishable, whereas agency is imperishable.
Only that effort which is directed toward an object is lost here;
when that is lost, the ignorant person thinks, "I am destroyed. (15)
But as for that inwardly directed state which is the locus of the quality of omniscience, its loss could never occur, because nothing else is perceived [in its place]. (16)
The perception of that [reality] is constant and never deviates from the three states;
it belongs eternally to the well-awakened one, and likewise to the Supreme at the beginning and the end.

Endowed with the supreme Śakti, whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, the All-pervasive Lord shines in two states; elsewhere, however, He is composed solely of consciousness.
The outflows of the vibration of qualities and so forth, having attained their own existence by relying upon the universal vibration, shall never be obstacles for the knower. (19)
But those of unawakened intellect, striving to conceal their own true state, cast others onto the terrible path of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross. (20)
Therefore, one who is constantly diligent in discerning the reality of vibration attains his own true nature even while awake before long.
Whether extremely angry or greatly delighted, or while reflecting "What shall I do?",
or while running— whatever step one takes, therein vibration is established.
Adopting this state of mind, he remains firm, having resolved: "Whatever he says to me, I shall certainly do. (23)
Relying upon that [channel], both the moon and the sun set on the upward path within the suṣumṇā,
leaving behind the domain of Brahmā’s mouth.
Then, in that great void where the moon and sun have dissolved,
the deluded one becomes awakened and unobscured, like the state of deep sleep.
The second is the outflow:
having ascended that power, the mantras, endowed with the power of omniscience, proceed for the sake of their respective functions, like the sense organs of embodied beings. (1)
Right there they are completely dissolved, tranquil in form and stainless; together with the mind of the worshipper, these possess the nature of Śiva.

Because the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything, since it arises from all states of being, by virtue of its nature as the consciousness thereof and through the realization of identity with that. (3)
Therefore, in the contemplations of word and meaning, there is no state that is not Śiva;
the enjoyer himself always abides everywhere in the form of the object of enjoyment.
Or he whose consciousness perceives the entire world as a play—he, constantly seeing thus and remaining disciplined, is undoubtedly liberated while living. // 5 //
This indeed is the arising of that object of meditation within the meditator's mind:
it is the attainment of identity with it for the practitioner who so desires. (6)
This alone is the attainment of the nectar of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self;
and this is the initiation into Nirvāṇa, which bestows the true being of Śiva. // 7 //
The third is the outflow:

just as the Creator, when requested according to one's desire, brings about for embodied beings the rising of the moon and sun so that they may attain the objects situated in their hearts while awake. // 1 //
Likewise, because he never fails to fulfill desired objects even in dreams, he who stands in the middle [of the path] must necessarily manifest [the truth] very clearly at all times. //2//
Otherwise, however, creation would be independent because it possesses that nature, just as the world-creation is constant in both the states of waking and dreaming for an ordinary person. (3)
For just as an object seen indistinctly, even when the mind is attentive, appears much more clearly later on when cultivated through the exertion of its own power; // 4 //
Likewise, whatever exists in its ultimate sense, by what means, where, and in what manner—that [reality], having been entered by power in that very way, proceeds forth before long. (5)
For even one who is weak proceeds toward his task by overcoming it;
likewise, one who is extremely hungry should conceal his hunger.
Just as omniscience and other qualities [arise] when the body is presided over by this [wisdom], so too will it be everywhere through such presiding over one's own self. (7)
Illness is a wasting away of the body, and its course proceeds from ignorance; if that [ignorance] is destroyed by the unfolding of consciousness, how could such illness exist without a cause? (8)
Since the arising of another thought occurs for one who is intent upon a single thought, that [arising] should be known as "unmeṣa" (opening); one should personally observe it.
From this [bindu] comes the drop (bindu), from this the sound (nāda), from this form, and from this taste; these proceed very quickly as the agitators of embodied beings. (10)
When one abides pervading all objects as if out of a desire to see them, then what is the use of much speaking? One will understand by oneself alone. // 11 //
Awakened, one should always remain having perceived the objective field through knowledge;
one should subsume everything within that single point, and thereby one is not afflicted by anything else.

Having fallen into the state of being an object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds, he whose power has been eclipsed by *kalā* is known as a bound soul (*paśu*). (13)

The depletion of the supreme nectar-essence that occurs for him through the arising of a cognition brings about his lack of autonomy; and that [cognition] has as its object only those [elements]. (14)
And its powers for veiling its own nature are ever-active, because the arising of cognition does not occur without the interpenetration of words. (15)
This power, consisting of action, belongs to Śiva; residing in bound souls (paśu), it is their binder, yet when established upon its own path and known, it brings about accomplishment. 16.

Constrained by the *puryaṣṭaka*— which consists of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), arises in the form of the mind and the sense of "I," and functions within the intellect— it experiences that which arises from those [elements], namely the emergence of objective cognitions.
Under the influence of that state, one experiences enjoyment while subject to another's power;
therefore, we shall now explain the cause for the cessation of this cycle of transmigration.

But when it has become firmly established in one [state], then by restraining its dissolution and emergence, one attains the state of the enjoyer; thereafter, one becomes the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara).
I pay homage to that wondrous speech of the Guru, which possesses diverse meanings and words, and is a boat for crossing the unfathomable ocean of doubt; this is the fourth outflow.
Even though this wealth of knowledge— which is difficult to attain— has been placed within the cave of the heart,
it leads to the welfare of all the world forever, just as it did for Vasugupta.
